summary: This unit teaches you to develop and implement organisational policies: to tell policies from procedures and guidelines; to find the need, research the law and evidence, and draft a clear policy; to consult, cost, check for fairness and get approval; to launch the policy with communication, training and updated procedures; and to monitor compliance, deal with exceptions and breaches, review the policy and withdraw it when it is out of date.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. An **organisational policy** is a formal statement, approved at a senior level, of what the organisation requires and why. Policies guide decisions and behaviour so that staff and managers deal with similar situations in the same fair way, and so that the organisation meets the law. At Level 5 you lead the development of policies in a ministry, agency, municipal corporation, hotel, school or business, and make sure they are used.
A policy that sits in a file does nothing. This unit covers the whole life of a policy: **need, research, drafting, consultation, approval, launch, monitoring, review and withdrawal**.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Tell policy, procedure, guideline and form apart, and explain how they fit with the law and the code of conduct.
Show when a policy is needed, and gather evidence, legal requirements and related policies.
Use a standard structure and plain, firm wording; name an owner; allow for exceptions.
Consult those affected, assess impact and fairness, cost the policy and get legal review.
Use the approval authority named in the framework and keep one numbered current version.
Launch, communicate and train, update procedures and forms, and register the policy.
Check compliance, handle exceptions and breaches fairly, measure effect and review or withdraw policies.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions, with short sums on costs, percentages and dates.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as procedure, breach, exception, version control) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks**: draft a short policy with its procedure and plan its consultation, launch and review.

blocks.note: Many questions ask what a policy officer should do next. The best answer is nearly always the one that is fair, follows the framework, uses evidence and is put in writing.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Policy, procedure and the policy framework

head: Document
What it is
Approved by
How often it changes
rows: A formal statement of **what** the organisation requires and **why**; applies widely
Senior level named in the framework (for example the Permanent Secretary, chief executive or board)
The **steps** for carrying out the policy: who does what, in what order, with which forms
The policy owner or a manager
Advice and good practice that helps staff apply the policy; not strictly binding, staff use judgement
A document used to carry out a procedure, such as a travel claim

blocks.p: Example: a travel policy says that official travel must be approved in advance and claims paid at an approved rate, because public money must be controlled. The travel procedure explains how to request approval, which form to use and when claims are due. A guideline suggests how to choose the cheapest suitable transport.

A **policy framework** is the set of rules for how policies are made, approved, published, reviewed and withdrawn in the organisation. It says who may approve what, the standard format, how long a policy lasts before review, where the register is kept and how versions are controlled.

blocks.h: Where policies sit in the legal and rules hierarchy

flow: Laws passed by Parliament and regulations
Public service rules and the code of conduct

ul: A policy must **follow the law**. If a ministry's policy on official vehicles conflicts with a law passed by Parliament, the law must be followed and the policy corrected, whoever signed the policy.
A policy must fit the public service rules and the code of conduct, which cover matters such as gifts, conflicts of interest and political neutrality.

A policy must be consistent with the other policies of the organisation. A remote-work policy that lets staff use their own laptops cannot sit beside an ICT security policy that forbids it. Check related policies and settle the conflict first.

blocks.p: Refer to laws by their **purpose** (employment law, the data protection law, procurement rules for public bodies). Do not quote sections.

ul: Fair and consistent treatment of staff and the public.
Legal compliance and protection from legal challenge.
Clear accountability: who decides and who is answerable.
Efficiency: staff do not have to invent answers each time.
Support for the organisation's strategic plan and values.

head: Trigger
Example
rows: Different offices handle the same request in different ways, and clients complain
A new law or a change in the law
New requirements on personal data or workplace safety
A record lost or a fraud found by internal audit
A new service, technology or risk
Online payments, social media, new premises
A gap shown by the plan or a review
A strategic objective with no rules to support it
A request from the board, Minister or staff
A staff association asks for a clear leave rule

blocks.p: A personal wish, such as a manager who wants staff to think better of her or a preference for a colour of file, is not a need. A need is a **problem or risk the organisation must manage**.

flow: Define the problem and who is affected
Check the laws, public service rules and existing policies that apply
Collect evidence: records, audit findings, complaints, costs
Look at how comparable organisations deal with it
Talk to the people who will use the policy

ul: **Evidence beats opinion.** To decide what an overtime policy should cover, use overtime records, audit findings and staff views. A rumour, one manager's opinion or a policy copied unchanged from a foreign company is not enough.
Before drafting a social media policy, first research **the laws, service rules and policies that apply**, not which platforms are most popular.
Check whether the problem needs a policy at all. Sometimes better training or clearer procedures are enough.

blocks.p: A policy that affects health and safety needs a working group with **managers, safety representatives, HR and legal**. Senior managers alone are quick but miss the front line; the legal unit alone knows the law but not the work; an outside consultant working alone does not know the organisation. Name a lead officer and a timetable.
Check each draft against the **strategic plan and values** so that it supports, and does not undermine, the organisation's aims. A policy does not replace the strategic plan.

head: Section
What it contains
rows: Title, number, version, approval date, owner, next review date
Why the policy exists, linked to an aim or a legal duty
Who and what it applies to, for example all permanent and temporary staff at every office
Terms that could be read in different ways, such as "official vehicle"
The rules, in short, clear, numbered sentences
Who owns the policy, who applies it, who monitors it
Who may approve a departure from the policy and on what grounds
How compliance is checked and what happens if the policy is breached
When and how it will be reviewed

ul: Use **firm, plain words**: "must", "must not", "may". "Personal data files must be locked away at the end of each day" is a good policy statement. "Staff should try, where they can, to maybe lock some files away" is not.
Write for the reader. Use short sentences and avoid legal terms where plain words do. A draft leave policy full of legal terms should be rewritten plainly and **tested on a few staff**.
Name the **policy owner**, the officer or post that keeps the policy current and answers questions.
Do not mix procedure into the policy. Put the steps in the procedure.

blocks.p: An **impact assessment** checks, during drafting, how the policy will affect different groups, such as women, people with disabilities, rural staff, staff with family or faith needs, and part-time workers. Ask:

ul: Does it unfairly exclude able people? A promotion rule that requires "at least ten years' service in Kingston" may exclude staff in other parishes.
Does it fit the staff and services? A requirement that all staff attend training on Saturdays needs a check on its effect on family and faith commitments.
Is it lawful, and is it consistent with the code of conduct and equality principles?
Is it practical and enforceable?

blocks.p: Estimate the cost before approval. A policy that cannot be funded will not be followed.

head: Item
Working
rows: Mileage: J$65 per km, 12 officers at 800 km a month
Telephone allowance: J$3,000 for 85 officers and J$5,000 for 15 supervisors
Training: J$2,500 per person for 240 staff plus J$150,000 for the trainer

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, for example by calculating the parts in two orders: 12 x 800 x 65 and 65 x 800 x 12. If the policy costs more than the budget, say so, and offer cheaper options.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A policy officer must write policies for the organisation, not for one person or unit. If a senior manager asks for an allowance policy to be worded so that only his own unit qualifies, the officer insists on fair criteria and, if pressed, raises the matter with a more senior officer or the proper channel. She does not do it quietly, and she does not go along because he is senior.

List the stages with their durations. If drafting ends on 1 June and the policy needs 3 weeks of consultation, 2 weeks to revise and 4 weeks for approval, that is 9 weeks, or 63 days, so approval could come on about 3 August.

head: Group
Why
rows: Staff and managers who will apply the policy
They know whether it can work in practice
Matters that affect conditions of service, such as shift patterns, may need consultation under agreements and employment law; it does not mean the union writes the policy
HR, finance, ICT, legal and other support units
Cost, systems, law, links to other policies
Where health and safety is affected
Where the policy changes services to the public

ul: Set a clear period (for example three weeks) and say what is open to change.
Use methods that suit each group: summary and online survey for all staff, meetings with supervisors, a formal meeting with the union.

Keep a **comments log**. If staff send in 40 comments, weigh each one, change the draft where justified, and report back what you changed and why. Do not accept every comment, ignore those you disagree with, or delete them.

blocks.p: The legal unit checks that the draft **fits the law and the service rules**. It checks, for example, that a discipline policy follows fair procedure, and that a CCTV policy respects the purpose of the data protection law: signs inform people, and footage is kept only as long as needed, not shared with anyone who asks, and cameras are not placed in private areas such as toilets. Legal review does not delay a policy to the next financial year or take over the HR work.

A new organisation-wide policy is approved by **the authority named in the policy framework**, not by whoever helped to draft it. Record the approval date, the version number and who approved it. A policy signed years ago by a chief executive who has left should be reviewed and re-signed by the current head.

**Version control** means the controls, such as version numbers, dates and a change history, that stop staff working from an old copy. If two versions of the leave policy with different rules are on the intranet, keep one approved, numbered version and remove the other.

blocks.note: The current policy is the only copy staff may use. Old versions are archived, not left on the intranet.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Approval is the start, not the end. Implementation turns the document into practice.

flow: Name the policy owner and enter it in the register
Publish the policy and a summary
Tell outside users where it affects them

ul: **Brief managers first.** They apply the policy in their units and answer questions.
Publish the approved policy on the **intranet**, with a short plain-language summary.
Do not rely on one email, a notice in a basement store room or on staff asking for it by name.
Ask staff to **sign that they have read and understood** the policy when this matters. It shows each officer received it and understood it.
If the policy changes how the public deals with the body, for example how to request copies of records, tell the public through the website and service counters.

blocks.p: Training should focus on **what staff now do differently, with practice**: for example how to handle cash at a service counter under the new policy. It should not tell the history of the topic, or who wrote the policy.

Update the procedure and the forms before launch. If the new travel policy no longer fits the old claim form, the form is updated, not used until stock runs out, annotated by hand or redesigned by each unit.

A **policy register** is a list of each policy with its number, owner, version, approval date and review date. Its main use is to track each policy's owner and review date. When the owner of a policy retires, **assign a new owner and update the register**.

head: Role
Responsibility
rows: Keeps the policy current, answers questions, gives rulings on meaning, reviews it
Applies the policy in the unit, briefs staff, deals with breaches
Know and follow the policy and report concerns
Tests the most important policies on a risk basis
Approves, resources and sets the example

blocks.p: If managers in two divisions read a clause differently, ask the **policy owner to rule**, then fix the wording at the next amendment, so that all apply it the same way.

Each policy should say how compliance will be checked and who is responsible. Methods: spot checks, records review, observation, reports and audit. Six months after a clean-desk policy starts, the manager does **spot checks and looks at incident reports**. Counting printed copies or asking the policy owner what she thinks does not show compliance, and waiting three years for the full review is too late.
The test of a policy is the change it makes. Choose a measure linked to the purpose:

head: Policy
Evidence that it works
rows: Complaints settled faster and fewer repeats (not a new logo, or staff saying that they have heard of it)
Fewer unauthorised trips, lower fuel costs

blocks.p: An **exception** is an approved departure from a policy for a particular case, given by the authority the policy names. A good policy sets an **exceptions process**: who approves and on what grounds. Refusing every request, letting everyone decide for themselves, or dropping the policy for anyone with a good reason are all poor answers. Example: office hours are 8:30 to 4:30, and an officer asks to work 7:30 to 3:30 to care for a parent. The exceptions process decides it on stated grounds and the decision is recorded.

A **breach** is an act that goes against a policy, such as using an official vehicle for a private trip. The manager should **apply the breach process fairly and record it**: establish the facts, give the officer a chance to respond, apply the proper step and keep the record. Ignoring it because the officer is popular, reprimanding loudly in front of the team, or changing the policy to allow the act are all wrong.

ul: Review on the **set review date**, for example every two or three years. A policy approved in March 2025 and reviewed every three years is due for review in March 2028.

Review **early** when a law changes, an incident shows the policy is not working, the organisation or its systems change, or audit finds a problem. Not when a photocopier arrives or the policy owner goes on leave.
A review asks whether the policy **still meets its purpose, the law and current practice**.
Collect evidence: monitoring data, exceptions, breaches, complaints, staff and union views.
Decide to keep, amend or withdraw.

blocks.p: If a policy is no longer needed, for example a policy on fax machines when none are used, **withdraw it formally and record the withdrawal** in the register. Do not delete it quietly, leave it in place or ask staff to go on following it. A **withdrawn** or rescinded policy is formally taken out of force.

blocks.h: Bringing a policy library under control

blocks.p: Where many policies are out of date, in conflict or unknown to staff: appoint a lead, make an inventory and register, sort policies (keep, merge, review urgently, withdraw), agree a framework with owners and review dates, and publish one current set.

blocks.note: Keep the cycle moving: need, research, draft, consult, approve, launch, monitor, review. The results of each review feed the next version.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: explain the difference between a policy, a procedure, a guideline and a form.
describe a policy framework and explain why the law always takes priority.
identify when a policy is needed and which evidence to research.
set up a drafting group with the right members.
draft a policy with the standard sections and plain, firm wording.
name a policy owner and write an exceptions process.
carry out an impact assessment for fairness.
cost a policy and work the sums twice.
plan consultation and deal with the comments.
explain legal review, approval authority and version control.
launch a policy with briefing, training, updated procedures and a register entry.
monitor compliance and deal with exceptions and breaches fairly.
measure whether a policy is working.
decide when to review early, and how to withdraw a policy.
act ethically when pressed to write a policy for one person's benefit.

terms: Policy
A formal statement of what the organisation requires and why.
Procedure
The step-by-step method for carrying out a policy.
Guideline
Advice that helps staff apply a policy but is not strictly binding.
Policy framework
The rules for how policies are made, approved, reviewed and withdrawn.
Scope
The section that says who and what the policy applies to.
Definitions
The section that explains terms used in the policy.
Policy owner
The officer or post that keeps the policy current and answers queries.
Impact assessment
A check of how a policy will affect different groups.
Version control
Version numbers, dates and change history that stop staff using an old copy.
Policy register
A list of policies with owner, version and review date.
Intranet
The internal website on which approved policies are published.
Exception
An approved departure from a policy in a particular case.
Breach
An act that goes against a policy.
Code of conduct
The standards of behaviour expected of public officers.
Withdrawn (rescinded)
Formally taken out of force and removed from the current register.

c1.title: A purchasing card policy
c1.text: A government agency in Kingston is drafting a policy on purchasing cards for 25 officers. The draft says that cards may be used only for approved purchases up to J$50,000 each, with receipts handed in weekly. Training will cost J$3,000 per cardholder plus J$40,000 for a facilitator. The policy officer, Ms Janelle Francis, finishes the first draft on 5 January and plans 2 weeks of consultation, 1 week to revise and 3 weeks for approval.

c2.title: A dress code for a municipal corporation
c2.text: A municipal corporation in St James wants a dress code policy. The draft requires closed shoes, long trousers or skirts, and no head coverings at the counter. Staff on the outdoor crew say the rules are unsuitable for the heat and for their work. A staff member who wears a head covering for faith reasons is concerned. The union has asked to be consulted.

c3.title: An anti-harassment policy launch
c3.text: A ministry has approved a new anti-harassment policy. It has 240 staff in Kingston, Montego Bay and Mandeville. HR plans an email, a notice board poster and a short video. By the end of the first month, 204 staff have signed that they have read the policy. A supervisor in Mandeville later tells a complaining officer that the policy does not apply to "friendly jokes".

c4.title: A messy policy library
c4.text: A municipal corporation in Clarendon has 50 policies. Nine are past their review date. The leave policy appears on the intranet in two versions with different rules. The policy on photocopier use refers to machines that were sold two years ago. The policy on gifts was approved in November 2024 and must be reviewed every three years.

c5.title: A study leave policy at work
c5.text: Two years ago an agency introduced a study leave policy. Resignations of qualified staff fell from 20 a year to 14. Some managers say the rules are unclear, and two managers in the western region have given the same request different answers. A new law on employment has since been passed.

questions.q: The cost of training the 25 cardholders is J$3,000 each plus J$40,000 for the facilitator. What is the total cost?
questions.why: 25 x J$3,000 = J$75,000; adding the J$40,000 facilitator fee gives J$115,000. Check: 75,000 + 40,000 = 115,000.

questions.q: If drafting ends on 5 January, about when could the policy be approved?
o: 16 February
19 January
23 February
2 March
questions.why: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 weeks = 42 days. 5 January plus 42 days is 16 February. Do the sum from the stages listed in the plan.

questions.q: The draft says cards may be used only for "approved purchases" but never explains what that means. Which section should explain it?
o: Scope
Review
Related documents
Definitions
questions.why: The definitions section explains terms that could be read in different ways. Without it, officers and managers may each decide what counts as an approved purchase.

questions.q: A manager asks Ms Francis to add steps on how to complete the card claim form. Where do they belong?
o: In the policy statements, so that they are binding
In the procedure that supports the policy
In the definitions section of the policy
In the title page details
questions.why: A policy states what and why; a procedure sets out the steps. Keeping steps in the procedure lets them change without changing the policy.

questions.q: The union asks to be consulted on the dress code. What is the best response?
o: Refuse, because policies are a decision for management alone to make
Let the union write the whole policy itself to save management time
Consult it, as the policy affects staff conditions, and weigh its views
Consult it only after the policy has already been approved
questions.why: Consultation is part of fair policy making and may be required by agreements and employment law. It does not mean the union writes the policy or that management must accept every view.

questions.q: The staff member who wears a head covering for faith reasons is worried. What should the policy officer do?
o: Carry out an impact assessment and revise the rule if it is unfair
Keep the rule, as a single case should not be allowed to change policy
Add a note that staff who have concerns about the rule may resign
Apply the rule and look at any complaints that arise in two years
questions.why: An impact assessment checks effects on different groups during drafting. A rule that unfairly affects a group may be unlawful or unjust and should be revised.

questions.q: Many crew members send comments on the draft. How should Ms Francis use them?
o: Accept every single comment, so that staff feel that they have been heard
Keep only the comments that came in from the managers
Record the comments but make no changes at all to the draft
Weigh each comment, change the draft where justified and report back
questions.why: Consultation must be real. Comments are weighed, the draft is changed where it is justified, and people are told what changed and why.

questions.q: The final dress code lets the head of a unit approve different dress for outdoor work. What is this called?
o: A breach procedure
An exceptions process
A policy withdrawal
A version change
questions.why: An exception is an approved departure from the policy for a particular case, given by the authority the policy names. It makes the policy workable.

questions.q: Which approach to the launch is best?
o: Send one email to all staff, since they are expected to read their mail
Rely on the poster in the corridor and on the short video
Brief managers first, train staff, publish a plain summary
Ask staff to approach HR if they want any further details
questions.why: A launch needs briefing for managers, training for staff and a clear summary. One email or poster does not make sure that people understand.

questions.q: 204 of the 240 staff have signed. What percentage is that, and what should HR do?
o: 85%; follow up with the other staff and offer sessions
85%; stop now, since most of the staff have signed
15%; start the whole sign-up again from the beginning
60%; extend the launch to the following year
questions.why: 204 / 240 x 100 = 85%. Signing shows each person received and understood the policy, so HR follows up the remaining 36 and offers briefing sessions.

questions.q: The Mandeville supervisor says the policy does not apply to "friendly jokes". What is the best action?
o: Let the supervisor interpret the policy in her own unit as she sees fit
Tell the officer that the supervisor is probably right about the jokes
Ask the staff in Mandeville to vote on what the policy means
Ask the policy owner to rule, then fix the wording if it is unclear
questions.why: Where there are different readings, the policy owner rules and the wording is clarified. Unit-by-unit readings defeat the purpose of a policy.

questions.q: A manager breaks the new policy. Which response is correct?
o: Ignore it, as it is only the manager's first mistake in the job
Apply the breach process fairly and record it, whoever the person is
Announce the breach at a staff meeting to make an example of him
Change the policy so that the manager's conduct is then allowed
questions.why: A breach is dealt with fairly and recorded. Ignoring it, shaming the person or changing the rules to excuse the act each undermine the policy.

questions.q: What is the best first step in bringing the corporation's 50 policies under control?
o: Withdraw every policy and ask the staff to write new ones for the corporation
Send each policy to the Mayor and councillors for approval once again
List every policy in one register with its owner and review date
Ask each unit to decide which of the policies it will choose to follow
questions.why: Control starts by knowing what exists. An inventory and register show owners, dates and conflicts, so that policies can be kept, merged, reviewed or withdrawn.

questions.q: The gifts policy lets staff keep gifts "of small value" but does not say what this means. What is the best fix?
o: Set a clear value limit and a way to declare gifts
Leave each officer to judge what is small
Ban every gift of any kind at once
Let managers decide each case without any written rule
questions.why: A policy statement must be clear enough to apply and check. A set limit and a declaration step give everyone the same rule and make breaches easy to see.

questions.q: The photocopier policy refers to machines the corporation sold two years ago. What should happen?
o: Leave it in place in case it is needed again at some later time
Delete the file quietly from the intranet and say nothing
Rewrite it for a type of printer that nobody has bought
Withdraw it formally and record the withdrawal in the register
questions.why: A policy that is no longer needed is withdrawn formally and the register updated. Quiet deletion leaves no record, and keeping it adds clutter.

questions.q: The gifts policy was approved in November 2024 with a three-year review cycle. When is the review due, unless an event requires it earlier?
o: November 2026
November 2027
November 2029
May 2025
questions.why: November 2024 plus three years is November 2027. An earlier review is needed if the law changes or an incident shows the policy is not working.

questions.q: Resignations fell from 20 to 14 a year. By what percentage did they fall?
questions.why: (20 - 14) / 20 x 100 = 30%. The percentage is calculated against the starting figure.

questions.q: Two managers gave different answers to the same study leave request. What does this show?
o: The wording or procedure may be unclear, so the owner should clarify it
Managers must always be left to use their own judgement on each request
The policy has failed completely and must now be dropped
The staff member should be allowed to choose the answer she prefers
questions.why: Inconsistent decisions suggest unclear wording or weak guidance. The policy owner clarifies and, if needed, amends the policy and procedure.

questions.q: The new employment law has been passed. What should the agency do about its policy?
o: Wait for the next review date before looking at it
Assume that it is still lawful, since it was approved
Withdraw it and rely on managers' judgement
Review it early to check that it still fits the law
questions.why: A change in the law is a reason for an early review. A policy that conflicts with the law cannot be enforced.

questions.q: Which evidence would best show that the study leave policy is working?
o: More copies of the policy have been printed for the offices
Fewer resignations, more staff qualified and consistent decisions
Staff say that they know the policy exists and where it is kept
The policy document has been given a new cover and logo
questions.why: Evidence of effect on the purpose, here keeping and developing qualified staff, shows that a policy is working. Awareness or appearance alone does not.
